rationale.text: Tile the M-dimension with factor 128 to create 512/128=4 tiles. This matches a typical GEMM block size that fits comfortably in the 49KB shared memory while giving enough work per tile to hide latency. 128 is a canonical GEMM tile size for Ampere.

Tile the N-dimension with factor 128 to create a 128×128 output tile per thread block. Combined with the i-tile of 128, each block computes a 128×128 output region. This maximizes arithmetic intensity (128*128 outputs vs 2*128*K loads) and is the standard Ampere GEMM block shape that fits in shared memory (128*128*2 bytes ≈ 32KB for fp16, well under 49KB).

Tile the K reduction axis with factor 32 to enable software pipelining of shared memory loads. A k-tile of 32 with 128×128 output block means each stage loads 128×32 + 32×128 = 8192 elements into shared memory (32KB for fp16), fitting within the 49KB budget. This is the standard Ampere GEMM stage size that enables double-buffering and hides memory latency.

Map the i (M) outer-tile loop to threadblock.y so each thread block handles a different row-tile. With 512/128=4 tiles in M and 4 in N, this creates a 4×4=16 threadblock grid covering all 30 SMs efficiently. Using .y for the M dimension follows the row-major convention and improves L2 cache locality for A-matrix accesses.

Map the j (N) outer-tile loop to threadblock.x so columns are spread across the x-dimension of the grid. Combined with i→threadblock.y, we get a 2D 4×4 threadblock grid launching 16 blocks across 30 SMs. The x-dimension for j aligns with contiguous column access in row-major B, improving memory coalescing.

Vectorize the j (N) inner loop with width 4 to issue 128-bit (4×fp32) or 256-bit wide memory loads/stores. This saturates memory bandwidth and maps to LDG.128 instructions on Ampere, giving 4× throughput on B-matrix loads and C-matrix stores while keeping register pressure manageable.
